issues.legal_issue: A delegated rule is invalid when it substitutes ad hoc control by a local officer for the system the authorized rule-maker was empowered to establish.
material_facts: The governing law authorized the Chief Commissioner to make rules establishing a proper system of conservancy, sanitation, and watch and ward at fairs.
The rules prohibited holding a fair without a permit and left the District Magistrate to decide whether an applicant could establish a proper system, without setting out that system in the rules.
The rules also allowed the District Magistrate to impose terms and conditions on permits.
issues.conclusion: The permit rules were ultra vires because the authorized rule-maker had delegated to the District Magistrate the task of determining the required system, and the rules instead created ad hoc control rather than establishing that system.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 40 and 41 of the Ajmer Laws Regulation of 1877, the Chief Commissioner could make rules establishing a system for conservancy, sanitation, and watch and ward at fairs, and could attach penalties to breaches. The rule-maker had to establish the system in the rules so those concerned could know and comply with it; the authority to make those rules could not be delegated to the District Magistrate. The Court also relied on Tahir Hussain v. District Board, Muzafarnagar, AIR 1954 SC 630.

predicates.delegated_rule_challenge: A court is reviewing a rule made under authority delegated by a legislature.
predicates.parent_authority_limited_to_establishing: The law authorizes the rule-maker to establish a defined system for safety or administration at public gatherings.
predicates.rule_leaves_system_to_local_officer: The rule does not establish the system but leaves a local officer to determine what system applicants must provide.

issues.definition: When a challenged delegated rule leaves the required system to a local officer rather than establishing it within the parent authority, the rule is ultra vires.

issues.legal_issue: A rule allowing a local officer to revoke a fair permit without reasons or prior notice is invalid when it gives uncontrolled power to prohibit an otherwise protected activity.
material_facts: The rules empowered the District Magistrate to revoke a permit without assigning reasons or giving previous notice.
The governing law required attention to conservancy and sanitation but did not otherwise restrict the right to hold a fair.
The land on which the fair was held belonged to the applicant, and holding the annual fair was an occupation or business.
issues.conclusion: The rule authorizing revocation without reasons or prior notice was ultra vires because it conferred absolute and arbitrary power to prohibit the exercise of constitutionally protected rights.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 19(1)(f) and 19(1)(g) protected the relevant rights to property and to carry on an occupation or business; restrictions had to satisfy Articles 19(5) and 19(6), respectively. The Regulation authorized rules addressing conservancy and sanitation, not an uncontrolled power to prohibit fairs. The Court held the unreasoned, no-notice revocation power ultra vires.

predicates.delegated_rule_challenge: A court is reviewing a rule made under authority delegated by a legislature.
predicates.rule_allows_unreasoned_revocation_withou: The rule permits an official to revoke a permit without giving reasons or prior notice.
predicates.underlying_law_allows_fairs_subject_to_s: The governing law permits the activity subject to specified safety or administrative requirements and does not otherwise authorize its prohibition.

issues.definition: If a challenged delegated rule permits revocation without reasons or notice while the governing law allows the activity subject to safety requirements, the revocation rule is ultra vires.

issues.legal_issue: A permit refusal is invalid when the officer rejects an application on a ground the governing rules do not authorize and no other valid law empowers the officer to impose the ban.
material_facts: The applicant sought a permit to hold a fair on land belonging to him.
The District Magistrate refused the application because permits were to be issued only to local bodies, not private individuals.
The permit rules addressed whether applicants could provide conservancy, sanitation, and watch and ward, and did not authorize rejection based on the applicant's private status.
The Court held that the rules were ultra vires to the extent indicated and that no other valid law empowered the District Magistrate to prohibit the fair.
issues.conclusion: The District Magistrate's refusal was invalid and was quashed because the rules did not authorize rejection on the stated ground and, without valid rules or another law, the officer had no power to prohibit the fair.
issues.legal_principle: An administrative officer may exercise only the authority conferred by valid law; rules limited to assessing arrangements for conservancy, sanitation, and watch and ward do not authorize refusal on a policy ground unrelated to those matters. Because the rules were ultra vires to the extent indicated and no other valid law supplied the power to impose the ban, the refusal could not stand. The Court referred to Tahir Hussain v. District Board, Muzafarnagar, AIR 1954 SC 630.

rule.if: permit_refusal_challenge and refusal_based_on_applicant_category and valid_rules_do_not_authorize_that_ground and no_other_valid_law_authorizes_the_ban

predicates.permit_refusal_challenge: A court is reviewing an official's refusal of an application for permission to carry on an activity.
predicates.refusal_based_on_applicant_category: The officer refused permission because of the applicant's category or status rather than the requirements governing the activity.
predicates.valid_rules_do_not_authorize_that_ground: The applicable valid rules do not authorize refusal on the ground the officer relied on.
predicates.no_other_valid_law_authorizes_the_ban: No other valid law gives the officer power to prohibit the activity on that ground.

issues.definition: When an officer refuses permission on an unauthorized ground and no other valid law empowers the ban, the refusal is invalid.
